q: How does the HHL-based Bayesian-GP inference compare against modern classical Bayesian-inference baselines (SGLD, HMC, stochastic variational inference) in both fidelity of the posterior and wall-clock time for kernel matrices in the 10^3-10^5 regime relevant to modern GP practice?
basis: The paper claims a polynomial asymptotic speedup but never benchmarks against 2018-era or later classical Bayesian inference. Our replication is a 2x2 primitive check; the asymptotic claim is untested empirically. Modern classical baselines (e.g., GPyTorch with SKI/KISS-GP, NumPyro HMC) would give a fair reference point.
next_steps: Pick a mid-size GP regression benchmark (e.g., UCI protein or elevators, N~10^4). Run: (a) exact GP with Cholesky, (b) SVI GP, (c) HMC over hyperparameters + exact posterior, (d) HHL-style noiseless simulator on the same kernel matrix using Qiskit-Aer statevector where feasible, or a numerical HHL proxy where not. Compare posterior mean/variance MSE and wall-clock. Free endpoints: local CPU / uicgpu A100 for classical; Qiskit-Aer statevector for HHL sim.

q: How does HHL fidelity scale on the paper's exact circuit under realistic noise models drawn from currently available IBM Quantum hardware (Heron, Eagle) rather than parametric depolarizing errors on retired IBMQX5?
basis: C4 (F=0.78 on IBMQX5) cannot be reproduced on the original device. Our depolarizing sweep at 5-10% brackets it, but modern IBM hardware has much lower per-gate error (~10^-3) and different dominant error channels (crosstalk, readout, coherent drift). A modern hardware or noise-model rerun would strictly strengthen the replication.
next_steps: Pull the current calibration NoiseModel from an IBM Quantum backend via qiskit-ibm-runtime (free tier, 10 min/month allotment). Rebuild the noise model and rerun the 2x2 HHL circuit; report fidelity vs the classical target. Then if the free tier allows, submit the actual 4-qubit circuit as a small job to a Heron-family device. Free endpoint: IBM Quantum Open Plan.

q: Does the quantum-Bayesian-GP predictive uncertainty remain well-calibrated when HHL post-selection failure and readout noise are folded into the posterior variance, i.e., do 95% credible intervals actually cover 95% of held-out points on a real dataset?
basis: We reproduce the numerical variance (0.6725) but never test coverage on real data. The paper does not either. Calibration is the practical distinguisher between 'Bayesian' and 'just-a-point-estimate-plus-error-bar' methods, and HHL-specific noise (finite-precision QPE, post-selection dilution) could bias the reported variance in principle.
next_steps: Take a small regression benchmark (Boston housing or synthetic 1-D Snelson), do leave-one-out CV. For each held-out point, compute HHL-predicted mean and variance under the noisy simulator (gate_noise 0.001-0.05), then measure empirical coverage of 68/95/99% credible intervals. Report reliability diagrams. Purely classical simulator, no cost.

q: Does the choice of Bayesian-inference kernel (RBF vs Matern vs periodic vs deep-NN limit kernel) change the effective condition number kappa(K + sigma_n^2 I) enough to break HHL's asymptotic advantage on realistic datasets, and can preconditioning (Nystrom, inducing points) restore it?
basis: HHL runtime scales with kappa, and Aaronson's fine-print critique of HHL centers on hidden kappa/preparation costs. The paper does not analyze kappa on any real dataset. This is the single most-cited theoretical caveat and it is directly testable.
next_steps: Load 3-5 standard GP-benchmark datasets, build K + sigma_n^2 I under RBF/Matern-3/2/Matern-5/2 kernels with reasonable hyperparameters (via marginal-likelihood maximization on a subset). Report empirical kappa distribution. Apply Nystrom / SKI / inducing-point preconditioning; report the reduced effective kappa. Fold into the theoretical HHL runtime formula and compare to classical Cholesky (kappa-independent). Pure CPU, free.

q: Can the paper's HHL-for-GP idea be extended to a hybrid classical-quantum active-learning loop, where the quantum inverter picks the next experimental query by maximizing predictive variance, and does this yield a wall-clock improvement over classical GP active learning on quantum-experiment-design tasks (e.g., variational-quantum-eigensolver ansatz search, quantum-optimal-control pulse shaping)?
basis: The paper stops at posterior inference. But GP posterior variance is the standard active-learning acquisition function, and quantum-experiment design (VQE, quantum control) is precisely the domain where the quantum-native posterior might most naturally couple. This is a concrete, testable extension no one has yet published to our knowledge.
next_steps: Pick a small VQE benchmark (H_2, LiH ansatz-parameter search) or a QOC pulse-shape task. Build a GP surrogate over the parameter landscape. Run classical GP active learning with expected-improvement / max-variance acquisition. Then replace the posterior-variance-evaluation step with the HHL-based inference from this replication (noiseless simulator at first). Compare number of queries to reach a target energy / fidelity. Free: local Qiskit-Aer + a classical VQE simulator.
